extracted.intended_audience: The people of the State of New York / citizens considering ratification of the proposed U.S. Constitution; informed public and political actors interested in constitutional structure
extracted.subtask_description: Examine and judge provisions of a proposed constitution with respect to the proper distribution of legislative, executive, and judiciary powers, the adequacy of checks and balances, and safeguards (militia, conventions) against usurpation. Applies to assessing whether concentration or mixing of powers threatens liberty and how to remedy encroachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as safeguard against a standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: A properly constituted militia, composed of a large proportion of citizens and officered by men chosen from among themselves and attached to local governments, provides a practical check on the federal standing army and is a primary safeguard of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text argues the highest sustainable standing army will be at most ~1/100 of the population (or 1/25 of those able to bear arms), yielding an army of ~25–30,000, opposed by a militia 'amounting to near half a million of citizens with arms in their hands'. Advantages cited: being armed, subordinate/local governments to rally and lead them, officers chosen by militia, and their attachment to local governments and popular confidence. Implication: reliance on a large popular militia and local governments reduces the danger from a federal standing army; fear of federal annihilation of state governments by military force is exaggerated. Anti-pattern: assuming a standing army will inevitably overpower militias without considering relative numbers, local attachment, and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: True meaning of the separation-of-powers maxim (Montesquieu)
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that 'legislative, executive, and judiciary departments ought to be separate and distinct' does not require absolute isolation of departments; it forbids the accumulation of the whole powers of more than one department in the same hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual guidance: citation of Montesquieu and the British constitution to show that partial agency or control between branches exists in practice (e.g., executive shares in treaty-making, judicial appointments by executive, legislative impeachment power). The proper test is whether ONE PERSON or BODY possesses the WHOLE power of another department. Anti-pattern: interpreting separation so strictly as to forbid any partial agency or constitutional control among departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial mixture of powers permissible so long as no whole power is consolidated
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial blending (e.g., appointment powers, qualified vetoes, impeachment jurisdiction) between departments is acceptable provided it does not amount to the consolidation of the entire executive, legislative, or judicial power in the same hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from state constitutions: executive may have a qualified negative on legislature; Senate may be court of impeachment; judges may be appointed by executive; legislature sometimes appoints officers. The allowance of these partial interconnections is consistent with Montesquieu's meaning when understood in context. Anti-pattern: treating any interconnection as a violation of the maxim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constitutional checks required beyond 'parchment barriers'
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal demarcations of departmental boundaries in a constitution are insufficient alone; the system must supply practical securities that enable each department to resist encroachments by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: experience shows legislative departments tend to expand their power and can evade 'parchment' boundaries; effective defense requires structural provisions (checks and balances) that work in practice. Evidence cited: state experiences (Virginia and Pennsylvania), Jefferson's critique, and Council of Censors findings where legislatures assumed executive and judicial functions. Anti-pattern: relying solely on written limits without institutional means to enforce them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative usurpation is the principal danger in a representative republic
rubrics_metrics.description: In a representative republic, the legislative branch poses the greatest risk of encroachment due to its extensive constitutional powers, ability to mask incursions under complex measures, access to public finances, and influence over appointments and salaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning: the legislature's scope is broader and less precisely limited than executive or judicial powers; it controls public money and can exert influence through pecuniary rewards. Examples: state records where legislatures drew judicial matters into their cognizance and varied judges' salaries. Implication: constitutional design should provide special guards against legislative overreach (not only against executive usurpation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutional dependence of judges and executive on the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges and executive officers should not be left dependent on the legislature for their subsistence or continuance in office, because such dependence facilitates legislative encroachment on their independent functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited abuses: instances where judges' salaries were altered, judges and executive officers made removable or appointed by legislature, and where legislature assumed powers that properly belong to the judiciary or executive. Design implication: fix tenure/salary/appointment structures to minimize legislative leverage over other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional road for popular appeal (convention) as extraordinary remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a clear constitutional mechanism to appeal to the people — e.g., calling a convention — for altering the constitution or correcting breaches when departments concur that it is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific proposal quoted: 'whenever any two of the three branches of government shall concur in opinion, each by the voices of two thirds of their whole number, that a convention is necessary for altering the constitution, or correcting breaches of it, a convention shall be called for the purpose.' Rationale: the people are the legitimate fountain of power and can adjudicate constitutional meaning. Caveats: (1) the mechanism fails if two departments combine against the third; (2) frequent appeals to the people risk undermining reverence for government and public tranquillity; therefore such appeals should be reserved for 'certain great and extraordinary occasions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret constitutional language in light of practical examples and historical usage
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying abstract political maxims, interpret their meaning by reference to historical examples (e.g., British constitution) and the practical sense in which authors like Montesquieu used them, rather than by literal or absolutist readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text uses comparative reasoning (British constitution, various state constitutions) to show how maxims were understood and implemented. Implication: constitutional critique should weigh practice and precedent to determine whether a provision truly threatens liberty or simply reflects necessary partial agency between branches.
